turns.prompt_text: I seen this product that allows you to use your Wi-Fi to be able to see exactly where people are in their house. Also, it measures their 17 points on their skeleton and I can see things like I think it was their body temperature or heart rate or something all through their Wi-Fi
turns.response_html:
The technology described is entirely real and has transitioned from academic research into actual production software. This field is known as Wi-Fi Sensing or Wi-Fi Doppler Imaging, and specific systems like WiFi DensePose and commercial edge frameworks like RuView do exactly what was observed.

It does not require optical cameras or thermal imaging. Instead, it relies purely on the physics of radio wave propagation.

How It Works: Channel State Information (CSI)

Standard Wi-Fi routers do not just transmit data; they constantly analyze how the signal bounces off the environment to maintain a stable connection. This diagnostic data is called Channel State Information (CSI).

When a person moves through a room, their body reflects, absorbs, and scatters these high-frequency radio waves. By processing these subtle signal disturbances through specialized deep learning models (such as WiFlow or DensePose architectures), systems can reconstruct physical states without capturing a single pixel of video.

1. The 17-Point Skeleton (Pose Estimation)

The "17 points" refer directly to the standard COCO (Common Objects in Context) keypoints used in computer vision to map the human skeleton (joints like shoulders, elbows, wrists, hips, knees, and ankles).

Instead of a camera feeding pixels to an AI, the Wi-Fi sensing system feeds the raw CSI phase and amplitude fluctuations into a neural network. The network maps how those radio waves are warped by human geometry and translates that deformation into real-time 3D coordinates. Because Wi-Fi signals easily penetrate standard drywall, wood, and concrete, this mapping works seamlessly through walls and in total darkness.

2. Measuring Heart Rate and Respiration

The tracking of vital signs relies on micro-movements and the concept of Fresnel zones (the concentric ellipses of radio wave propagation between a transmitter and receiver):

  • Breathing Rate: As a person breathes, their chest wall displaces by roughly 1 to 5 mm. This cyclical movement causes a periodic shift in the Wi-Fi signal's amplitude, typically falling into a low-frequency band of 0.1 to 0.5 Hz (6 to 30 breaths per minute).
  • Heart Rate: The blood pumping through arteries causes minute, sub-millimeter surface displacements on the body (0.1 to 0.5 mm). Advanced signal processing isolates these incredibly faint, higher-frequency vibrations (0.8 to 2.0 Hz) using phase-drift analysis and fast Fourier transforms (FFT) to calculate beats per minute.

Correction on Body Temperature: While the system can accurately track positioning, movement, breathing, and pulse, it cannot measure body temperature. Thermal tracking requires infrared/optical sensors. Wi-Fi signals cannot read the thermodynamic energy or infrared emission of skin; they only measure physical boundary displacement and mass.

Technical Architecture & Deployment

What makes this shift notable is the hardware footprint. It no longer requires massive enterprise radar rigs; it runs locally on commodity microcontrollers.

LayerComponentFunction
Edge HardwareCommodity chips (e.g., ESP32-S3)Captures raw 20 Hz CSI frames directly from the radio environment. Cost is under $10 per node.
Signal ProcessingRust-based FFT & FIR Bandpass FiltersFilters out ambient static noise and isolates the specific frequencies of human movement.
Inference ModelEncoder-Decoder Networks (e.g., 2.2M - 4.8M parameters)Decouples spatial-temporal features to output the 3D skeleton coordinates and vital sign metrics.
Output / IntegrationLocal API / MQTT / WebSocketsStreams coordinate payloads to visualization tools (like Three.js) or smart home hubs (like Home Assistant) with sub-50ms latency.

Because the raw data consists entirely of radio wave properties rather than images, developers position it as a privacy-preserving alternative for environments like eldercare facilities or smart homes, where cameras are invasive but automated fall detection and health monitoring are critical.

turns.prompt_text: So my basic thoughts on it are I would definitely like to use it. I'm very wary that there's definitely security concerns with this and I wonder the legalities of the situation. If I could do it myself I totally would but I fear for the legalities of privacy I would do it for my own Wi-Fi of course
turns.response_html:
The instinct to pause and evaluate the security and legal landscape here is entirely justified. When technology shifts from tracking devices (like logging a MAC address connecting to a router) to tracking physical matter (reconstructing human bone structure via passive radio disruption), it crosses a massive philosophical and legal boundary.

If a system like this is deployed strictly inside a private home, using a self-hosted environment, the immediate legal and security realities break down into specific categories.

The Legal Framework: A Mass Regulatory Blindspot

The core paradox of Wi-Fi sensing is that the technology has completely outpaced the law. Existing privacy frameworks were built around optical data and data packets—neither of which apply here.

1. The Statutory "Grey Zone"

  • The Wiretap Act & Electronic Communications Privacy Act (ECPA): These federal laws govern the interception of wire, oral, or electronic communications. However, Wi-Fi sensing doesn't intercept the payload or content of data packets. It doesn't read emails or listen to traffic. It merely measures how radio waves scatter off physical surfaces. Because you are measuring environmental mechanics rather than reading data traffic, standard wiretapping statutes generally do not apply.
  • Biometric & Camera Laws: Current privacy regulations (like Illinois’ BIPA or Europe's GDPR) heavily restrict unauthorized facial recognition and video surveillance. But because Wi-Fi sensing does not capture pixels, images, or unique biometric signatures (like a fingerprint or iris scan), it slips past most statutory definitions of "surveillance."

2. The Reasonable Expectation of Privacy (The Real Boundary)

Under U.S. common law, legal liability for domestic tracking usually hinges on a "Reasonable Expectation of Privacy" (Tort of Intrusion upon Seclusion).

  • Inside Your Own Home: If you own or lease the property and live alone, you have full legal authority to monitor the space. Deploying this on your personal network to track your own movements is completely legal.
  • Guests, Roommates, or Tenants: This is where the legal ice gets thin. If a guest, partner, or roommate enters the home, they have a reasonable expectation that they aren't being tracked down to a 17-point skeleton or having their respiration rate analyzed without consent. Even if no camera exists, if a dispute arose, a court could view unconsented, high-precision physical tracking through walls as a highly offensive invasion of privacy.

Security Risks of RF-Sensing Environments

From an engineering perspective, turning an environment into an active RF-sensing grid introduces severe, unique security vectors that go far beyond standard network vulnerabilities.

1. Plaintext Signal Exposure (The Physical Leaking of Data)

In standard Wi-Fi setups, while your internet traffic is encrypted (via WPA2/WPA3), the underlying radio behavior is completely exposed. Devices constantly transmit Beamforming Feedback Information (BFI) and CSI packets in plaintext so routers can mechanically steer signals.

The Risk: An attacker does not need to crack your Wi-Fi password to map your house. If they place a passive, specialized receiver within radio range outside your home, they can capture the exact same raw CSI fluctuations bouncing out through your windows and walls. They can run those frames through their own model to see where you are standing, if you are sleeping, or if the house is empty—all without ever authenticating onto your network.

2. Device Impersonation & Spoofing

If the hardware processing the skeleton mapping (such as an ESP32 edge node or a local server) relies on unauthenticated local broadcasts (like basic UDP streams or unencrypted MQTT topics), a malicious actor on the local network can easily spoof the payload. They could inject artificial CSI anomalies to mimic human presence, blinding or triggering smart home security systems.

3. Deep Learning Vector Vulnerabilities

Because the 17-point pose estimation relies on deep learning models to translate raw radio phases into coordinates, it is susceptible to adversarial environmental attacks. Moving large metallic objects, deploying specific active radio jams, or introducing conflicting high-frequency noise can cause the inference model to hallucinate positions or completely fail to detect movement.

Rules of Engagement for a Self-Hosted Setup

If you decide to prototype a system like this for personal use, you can mitigate almost all legal and security exposure by adhering to a strict deployment paradigm:

  • Air-Gap or Local Isolation: Never let the raw CSI stream or the inference coordinates leave the local network. Do not route the payloads through cloud-dependent smart home integrations. Keep the processing pipeline entirely on a local server or isolated VLAN.
  • Opt-In and Transparency: If anyone else lives in or frequently visits the space, treat the system exactly like an internal security camera. Explicitly inform them that the radio environment maps physical positioning, and provide a physical kill-switch (like cutting power to the sensing nodes) to completely disable the tracking layer when requested.

As you "tweak" your own version, you’ll find that the real magic isn't in the radio itself, but in the Signal Processing Pipeline. Here is how you might structure your own system:

Phase 1: Data Acquisition (The Hardware)

Phase 2: The "17-Point" Inference

You don't need to write the AI from scratch. You can use a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) or a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network.

  1. Input: 3D Tensor of CSI (Amplitude + Phase over time).
  2. Model: Map the tensor to a 1D vector of 34 coordinates ($17 \text{ points} \times 2 \text{ coordinates}$).
  3. Visualization: Use p5.js (since you already use it for MIDI) to draw the skeleton. You can literally pipe your RF data into a p5.js canvas to see your skeleton move in real-time.

Phase 3: The "Vital Signs" Filter

To get the heart rate, you’ll need to implement a Bandpass Filter.

  • Respiration: Filter for signals between 0.1 Hz and 0.5 Hz.
  • Heart Rate: Filter for signals between 0.8 Hz and 2.5 Hz.
  • Formula: You’ll likely use a Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) to find the dominant frequency in those narrow windows.

$$f_{bpm} = f_{Hz} \times 60$$

The "Jarvis" Approach to Privacy

If you’re worried about the legalities, the best engineering solution is Edge-Only Processing. By ensuring your software runs entirely on your Mac Mini or a Raspberry Pi and never sends the "pose" data to a cloud server, you technically and legally mitigate the biggest privacy risks. You aren't "transmitting" surveillance; you are just processing your own radio environment locally.

turns.prompt_text: So the product I saw which was ariel ai/cognitive systems use a wifi router, I'm not sure which models or vendors rhey support however, I'm very unsure of the hardware requirements to do something like this for them. They were just using one device that was already built in is how they pitched it
turns.response_html:
The single-device pitch is exactly how Cognitive Systems scales their business model. They operate purely as an enterprise software and IP layer, licensing their technology (WiFi Motion™) to internet service providers (ISPs) and chipset manufacturers.

The strategy relies on a key piece of network engineering: if you already have a router and a few connected devices in the house, you already have a multi-node tracking grid.

The hardware mechanics and vendor ecosystem break down into specific operational layers.

1. The Single-Device Illusion: How It Deploys

When a consumer buys into a "single-device" solution, the router itself isn't acting alone to map space. It requires at least one other Wi-Fi client in the environment to create a signal path.

  • The Tx/Rx Loop: The router acts as the central transceiver. It uses the background traffic of the devices already connected to it—like a smart TV, a phone on a charger, or a smart plug across the room—as the nodes of the grid.
  • The Mesh Advantage: If the user has a modern mesh router network (such as two or three access points spread across the house), the system becomes highly accurate because it actively measures the paths between those access points.

2. Supported Vendors and Ecosystems

Cognitive Systems integrates directly into the software stacks used by tier-1 ISPs and consumer hardware giants. The software is embedded at the firmware layer via open-source router frameworks like RDK-B (Reference Design Kit for Broadband) and prpl Foundation architectures.

The consumer-facing implementations usually appear under branded names:

  • Plume HomePass: Plume designs the cloud-coordinated mesh pods used by dozens of major ISPs. Their "Guard" and "Sense" features utilize this exact technology.
  • Xfinity (Comcast) Home Awareness: Because Comcast uses RDK-B gateways (like the XB7 and XB8 routers found in millions of homes), they can deploy this tracking capability via a standard, over-the-air firmware update without changing the consumer's physical box.
  • TP-Link Deco & Linksys Velop: Select high-end consumer mesh systems come with native "Wi-Fi Sensing" toggles built right into their management apps, processing the spatial calculations locally on the router's CPU or offloading the tensors to an integrated cloud API.

3. The Bare-Minimum Hardware Requirements

To run this kind of inference pipeline on a standard consumer device, the hardware requirements are lower than one might assume, because the heavy mathematical lifting is done on highly optimized data arrays:

  • The Wireless Chipset: This is the absolute bottleneck. The router must feature a chipset that exposes CSI (Channel State Information) extraction to the firmware. Major wireless silicon providers like Qualcomm (Immersive Home platforms), Broadcom, and MediaTek have native silicon support for this.
  • Standard-Essential Compliance (802.11bf): The wireless industry finalized the IEEE 802.11bf standard. This formalizes Wi-Fi Sensing as a native protocol layer. Any router certified for Wi-Fi 7 or late-stage Wi-Fi 6E typically has the physical capability built directly into the radio components.
  • Memory & Processing Footprint: Because the software filters out raw data down to essential phase/amplitude vectors before running the spatial model, it can run on dual-core ARM processors (common in modern routers) with as little as 512MB to 1GB of system RAM.

The Reverse-Engineering Approach

Subscribing to a service like Plume HomePass or enabling it on a compatible ISP gateway is an effective way to analyze the system's behavioral thresholds. By setting a device to log local packet distributions or monitoring how the management app interfaces with local network traffic, one can glean exactly how frequently the nodes ping each other to maintain a stable skeleton baseline.

turns.prompt_text: So this sounds like something where they have a deal with the network provider in order to be able to do this. This isn't something that I can really DIY
turns.response_html:
The corporate pitch makes it sound like a proprietary magic trick tied directly to an internet service provider contract. In reality, it is completely achievable to build a setup like this independently.

A massive open-source movement exists around this exact technology. The commercial versions just package it neatly. If a developer wanted to build an independent, privacy-focused alternative that does not rely on ISPs or cloud servers, the tools are completely accessible.

The Open-Source Reality: You Can Absolutely DIY It

The belief that this requires enterprise-grade hardware or backend ISP cooperation is a common misconception. The open-source community has already reverse-engineered and democratized the entire pipeline.

  • The Hardware Costs Under $10: You do not need to hack a locked-down ISP router. The exact same Channel State Information (CSI) frames can be extracted using basic, consumer-accessible microcontrollers like the ESP32-S3. These chips feature a native programming interface (esp_wifi_set_csi_rx_cb) that exposes the raw radio data directly.
  • Production-Ready Repositories Exist: Frameworks like RuView and WiFi-DensePose are open-source and active on GitHub. They are designed explicitly to take raw CSI data streams from cheap ESP32 nodes and pipe them into local servers (like a Raspberry Pi or a Mac Mini) via Docker.
  • The AI Models Are Public: You don't have to train a neural network to recognize a skeleton. Pre-trained lightweight models (like WiFlow or quantized DensePose variants) are hosted publicly on Hugging Face. These models take the phase and amplitude shifts from your local radio environment and map them directly into coordinates.

How an Independent Architecture Looks

An independent deployment bypasses the ISP entirely by creating a dedicated, local "radar" mesh that has nothing to do with standard internet traffic.

+------------------+         +-------------------+         +---------------------+
| ESP32 Sensing    |         | Isolated Local    |         | Web Application     |
| Nodes (Radio)    | ------> | Server (Inference)| ------> | UI Canvas           |
| Captures raw CSI |   UDP   | Runs 8KB Model    | WebSock | Renders 17-Point    |
| frames at 20 Hz  |  Stream | via Docker/Python |  Stream | Skeleton (p5.js)    |
+------------------+         +-------------------+         +---------------------+

1. The Edge Nodes (Data Capture)

Instead of relying on a single router, an independent setup uses 2 to 4 small ESP32 boards positioned in the corners of a room. One acts as a simple transmitter, and the others act as receivers. They ping each other at a steady 20 Hz rate, creating a dense web of invisible radio paths crossing the living space.

2. The Local Processing Layer

The edge nodes stream their raw binary payloads over a local network via UDP directly to a central machine. Because the mathematical models have been highly optimized and compressed, running the spatial calculations does not require a massive data center:

  • A 4-bit quantized version of the tracking model takes up less than 8 KB of space.
  • The inference pipeline can process frames in microseconds, meaning a basic local computer can handle the calculations easily without breaking a sweat.

3. The Visual Presentation Layer

Once the local server translates the radio noise into standard coordinates, it broadcasts the payload via WebSockets. A lightweight front-end framework can instantly pick up those data streams. Drawing the resulting coordinates onto a clean canvas is incredibly straightforward—making it a perfect use case for custom visual rendering environments like p5.js.

Where the DIY Complexity Lies

While the hardware is cheap and the software is available, executing this successfully requires careful tuning. Achieving a reliable setup involves working through a few key engineering realities:

  • Environmental Calibration: Radio waves are chaotic. A metal filing cabinet, a large mirror, or even a running microwave can alter how signals bounce. Building an independent system requires running a 30-to-60-second baseline calibration when the room is completely empty, allowing the software to subtract the static background noise.
  • Signal Diversity: A single node can easily detect if a room is occupied or track basic breathing patterns. However, accurately resolving a full 3D skeleton requires spatial diversity. It takes multiple physical angles to separate the signal reflections of individual limbs and prevent the tracking from collapsing into a single point.

Building an independent version allows for complete control over the data pipeline. It ensures that the room-mapping data never leaves the local network, turning a potential privacy risk into a secure, self-hosted tracking environment.

turns.prompt_text: Could I do this using my raspberry Pi Pico Wi-Fi enabled devices?
turns.response_html:
Using the Raspberry Pi Pico W for Wi-Fi sensing is technically possible, but it is a much more difficult path than using an ESP32-S3.

While the Pico W is a powerhouse for most IoT tasks, its wireless chip (the Infineon CYW43439) is less "open" than the Espressif chips when it comes to the specific sub-layer required for this project: Channel State Information (CSI) extraction.

The Technical Hurdles with Pico W

To map a 17-point skeleton, you need the raw CSI data. Most Wi-Fi sensing projects shy away from the Pico W for three specific reasons:

  1. Driver Limitations: The standard Pico W firmware and libraries (like network in MicroPython or the C SDK) do not currently provide a native function to "dump" CSI frames. On an ESP32, this is a single function call. On a Pico W, you would likely need to write custom firmware for the Infineon chip or use a modified driver, which is a significant "deep end" task.
  2. Processing Overhead: Extracting and piping raw RF data at 20-40 Hz requires a high-performance wireless stack. The Pico W's wireless chip handles a lot of the stack internally, which is great for stability but bad for researchers who want to "peek" at the raw radio waves.
  3. Community Support: Because the ESP32-CSI-Tool and RuView have been built specifically for Espressif hardware, you would essentially be building your own CSI extraction toolkit from scratch for the RP2040/Infineon architecture.

How You Could Still Use Your Pico W

If you are committed to using your Pico W boards, you can still participate in the architecture, but their role would change from being the Sensing Nodes to being the Data Integrators.

Path A: The "Hybrid" Setup (Recommended)

You use a single, cheap ESP32-S3 to act as the primary "Radar" (the one doing the CSI capture) and use your Pico W boards as the clients.

  • The Pico W's Role: It acts as a stationary Wi-Fi client. By simply pinging the router or the ESP32, the Pico W creates the "shadow" in the radio environment.
  • The ESP32's Role: It captures how the Pico W's signals are warping and sends that data to your Mac Mini for the 17-point skeleton processing.

Path B: The "Pico-as-Visualizer"

Since you enjoy building custom tools, you could use a high-powered machine (like your Mac Mini) to do the RF math and then stream the coordinates to the Pico W.

  • The Pico W could then drive a small OLED display or an LED matrix that shows a simplified stick figure of whoever is in the room. This moves the "visual coding" logic you like (similar to your p5.js work) onto the Pico.

Comparison: Pico W vs. ESP32 for RF Sensing

FeatureRaspberry Pi Pico WESP32-S3 (The "Gold Standard")
CSI ExtractionVery Difficult (No native API)Easy (Native API support)
ToolingMinimal for RF SensingExtensive (WiFi-DensePose, RuView)

Best Use CaseControl logic / UI / Simple IoTRF Sensing / Radar / AI Inference

Next Steps for an "Ames Surplus" Build

Since you frequently visit the ISU Surplus, keep an eye out for Intel 5300 Wi-Fi cards or old Atheros-based routers. These are essentially the "holy grail" of DIY Wi-Fi sensing because they allow for massive amounts of CSI data to be pulled into a Linux machine (like your Mac Mini) with almost no friction.

If you want to start today with what you have, I’d suggest setting up one Pico W to just "spam" the network with small pings while you use a laptop or Mac to see if you can "see" those pings fluctuating in Wireshark. It won't give you a 17-point skeleton yet, but it will let you see the "heartbeat" of your Wi-Fi environment.

Are you more interested in the software-side (writing the math to turn signals into skeletons) or the hardware-side (getting the raw radio data out of the chip)?

turns.prompt_text: I'm very unsure of what's in a Wi-Fi module anyways. I don't know the difference in quality of them. I've pulled one apart but I really don't know what's going on in there is. Would it be possible just to power the thing and plug it into my computer and start sensing?
turns.response_html:
To a software engineer, a Wi-Fi module is essentially a specialized SDR (Software Defined Radio) trapped in a very small, highly optimized cage.

When you pulled that module apart, what you saw was likely a sandwich of three distinct engineering layers. Understanding these layers is the key to why some modules can "see" people and others can't.

1. The Anatomy of a Wi-Fi Module

  • The RF Front-End (The "Ears"): This is the physical radio. It includes the antenna and the Low Noise Amplifier (LNA). Its job is to pluck incredibly faint 2.4 GHz or 5 GHz waves out of the air and amplify them without adding too much noise.
  • The Baseband Processor (The "Translator"): This is the "brain." It contains a DSP (Digital Signal Processor) that takes those raw analog waves and turns them into digital 1s and 0s. This is where CSI (Channel State Information) lives.
  • The MAC/Interface Layer: This manages the "handshaking" and data flow (TCP/IP) so your computer sees a network connection rather than raw radio static.

2. Can you just "Power and Plug"?

Short answer: No, not with a standard internal module.

Internal Wi-Fi modules (like the ones in laptops) typically use a PCIe or M.2 interface. You cannot simply solder a USB cable to them and expect them to work. USB and PCIe use entirely different electrical protocols and voltages.

The Better DIY Path: Instead of fighting with an internal module, you can achieve your "power and plug" goal by using a USB Wi-Fi Adapter or a Development Board.

  • Option A: High-End USB Adapter (The Intel 5300/Atheros Path): Certain older USB adapters (or M.2 modules in a PCIe-to-USB enclosure) are "legendary" because their drivers have been cracked open to let you stream raw CSI data directly to your Mac Mini.
  • Option B: The $10 ESP32-S3 (The "Jarvis" Path): This is currently the gold standard for DIY Wi-Fi sensing. You plug it into your computer via USB, flash it with sensing firmware (like RuView), and it immediately starts outputting the radio fluctuations you need to map a room.

3. Why Quality Matters for "Seeing" People

In a standard module, the hardware is designed to ignore noise. But for Wi-Fi sensing, the "noise" is the data.

FeatureCheap "Consumer" ModuleHigh-Quality "Sensing" Module
Antenna Count (MIMO)1 (SISO). Hard to get 3D depth.2 or 4 (MIMO). Allows for "triangulation" of limbs.
CSI AccessBlocked. Only gives you "Signal Strength."Open. Gives you Phase and Amplitude for every sub-carrier.
Sampling RateSlow. Might miss a heartbeat.High (up to 100Hz). Can "see" the micro-vibrations of a pulse.

Analogy: Using a cheap Wi-Fi module for sensing is like trying to read a book using a flickering flashlight. A high-quality module (like an ESP32-S3 or a Wi-Fi 7 chip) is like turning on the overhead lights—the environment becomes clear because you have more "perspectives" (antennas) and a higher "frame rate" (CSI resolution).

Your "Weekend Project" Recommendation

Since you have a Mac Mini and a Raspberry Pi, don't bother trying to rewire a salvaged module.

  1. Grab an ESP32-S3 dev board.
  2. Plug it into your Mac Mini via USB.
  3. Clone a repo like RuView or WiFi-DensePose.
  4. Run their local Docker container.

This will give you the "Power and Plug" experience you're looking for, and you can start seeing your own "17-point skeleton" on your screen in about 20 minutes.

Do you have any old routers or USB Wi-Fi dongles lying around? I can help you check if their chipsets are "sensing-ready."

turns.prompt_text: Why would I purchase a Wi-Fi module at a Goodwill or I was at surplus if I can to use it
turns.response_html:
The intuition here is spot-on. Finding a standalone Wi-Fi module at a place like a surplus outlet or Goodwill and trying to use it for an advanced RF-sensing project is a recipe for frustration. Without the right context, it is essentially e-waste.

The reasons why someone would buy old networking gear for this kind of project come down to specific hardware targets, and understanding them explains why a cheap development board is usually the better choice.

1. The "Hidden Treasure" Factor: Chipset Hunting

Engineers who scavenge thrift stores and surplus piles for Wi-Fi gear aren't looking for just any random card; they are hunting for specific, obsolete network chips that accidentally became the "holy grail" of radio research.

  • The Intel 5300 & Atheros AR9580: These specific internal Wi-Fi cards from over a decade ago are famous in the computer science community.
  • Why they are hunted: Modern consumer Wi-Fi cards completely lock down their raw radio data at the hardware level for security and stability. However, early researchers cracked open the firmware for these specific older Intel and Atheros chips, creating open-source tools (like the Linux 802.11n CSI Tool) that allow them to output raw Channel State Information (CSI) with zero hardware restrictions.
  • The Catch: If a buyer doesn't know the exact serial numbers and chipset models to look for, a salvaged module is virtually useless for sensing, as its locked-down firmware will hide the precise radio data required to map a room.

2. The Form Factor Nightmare

Even if a scavenger finds one of these legendary research chips, getting it to talk to a modern computer is an uphill battle.

  • Interface Incompatibility: Older high-end modules use legacy enterprise slots (like Mini-PCIe). A modern computer or laptop cannot accept them directly.
  • The Necessary Bridge: To actually use one, it has to be mounted into a desktop motherboard or placed inside a specialized Mini-PCIe to USB adapter board. It is never a simple "plug in and play" scenario.

3. Why the $10 Dev Board Won the DIY Scene

The open-source community largely stopped scavenging for old enterprise network cards because microcontrollers like the ESP32-S3 completely democratized the technology.

[Old Surplus Method]
Scavenge Old Card -> Buy Mini-PCIe to USB Adapter -> Install 10-Year-Old Linux Kernel Drivers -> Chaotic Real-Time Data

[Modern ESP32-S3 Method]
$10 Microcontroller -> Standard USB-C Cable -> Flash Open Firmware (e.g., RuView) -> Clean WebSocket Stream

Instead of fighting with outdated operating system drivers and complex hardware adapters to repurpose an old router card, a modern developer can buy a dedicated micro-development board for the price of a sandwich.

These modern chips have native software hooks designed specifically to output clean CSI data. They plug directly into a computer using a standard USB-C cable and handle the radio processing automatically.

The Verdict on Scavenging

Unless a project requires hunting down specific vintage hardware for academic replication, bypassing the surplus bins for the primary sensing nodes is usually the best approach. Grabbing an inexpensive, modern development board provides an immediate, reliable USB-to-computer connection, allowing the focus of the project to remain entirely on the software, the signal processing, and the visual mapping.

turns.prompt_text: I have some Nordic nrf 52. I have the development board and I have the dongle. Would those help?
turns.response_html:
The short answer is: No, the nRF52 series alone cannot perform Wi-Fi sensing. While the Nordic nRF52 (like the nRF52840) is a world-class piece of engineering for Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE), Thread, and Zigbee, it physically lacks a Wi-Fi radio. Since Wi-Fi sensing relies on the specific physics of 20MHz or 40MHz Wi-Fi OFDM signals, a Bluetooth chip simply doesn't have the "resolution" or the right frequency protocols to see the 17-point skeleton you're after.

However, since you have the development board and the dongle, they aren't useless for this project—they just play a different role than the "radar" nodes.

Why the nRF52 Can't "See" Skeletons

The mapping technology we discussed requires Channel State Information (CSI).

  • Wi-Fi CSI: Analyzes 64 to 128 individual sub-frequencies (subcarriers) simultaneously. This is what allows the AI to "see" the difference between a shoulder and an elbow.
  • nRF52 (BLE): Operates on a single, narrow channel at a time. It's like trying to see a high-definition 3D movie through a keyhole. It can tell if a signal is getting weaker (RSSI), but it can't map the physical geometry of a human body.

How You Could Use Them in Your Setup

Since you have a Development Board (DK) and a Dongle, you can use them to build the "Last Mile" of your sensing system:

1. The "Notification" Node (The Dongle)

You can use your Mac Mini to do the heavy Wi-Fi math (using an ESP32 as the sensor). Once the Mac identifies a skeleton or a specific movement, it can send a command via Bluetooth to your nRF52 Dongle plugged into a different device (like a lamp or a remote screen) to trigger an action.

Jarvis Analogy: The Wi-Fi (ESP32) is the "eyes" in the ceiling; the nRF52 Dongle is the "finger" that flips the light switch.

2. The "Vital Signs" Dashboard (The DK)

If you build a p5.js dashboard on your Mac, you could use the nRF52 Development Board to drive a physical "health monitor" on your desk.

  • Use the DK to drive an LCD or a series of LEDs that pulse in sync with the heart rate detected by your Wi-Fi sensing grid.
  • Because the DK has a built-in Segger J-Link debugger, it’s great for prototyping these kinds of hardware-to-software bridges.

3. High-Precision "Direction Finding" (The Bluetooth 5.1 Factor)

If your boards are nRF52811 or nRF52833, they support Angle of Arrival (AoA). This is a different kind of sensing.

  • While Wi-Fi sensing is "device-less" (the person doesn't need a phone), nRF52 direction finding is "device-based."
  • If you carry the nRF52 Dongle in your pocket, the DK can track your exact X/Y coordinate in a room with centimeter-level accuracy by measuring the phase of the Bluetooth signal. It’s a great fallback if the Wi-Fi skeleton tracking gets too "noisy."

The "Ames Surplus" Upgrade

If you want to use your Nordic ecosystem for Wi-Fi, keep an eye out for the nRF7002 Expansion Shield at the ISU Surplus. Nordic recently released the nRF7002, which is their first actual Wi-Fi chip. It’s designed to plug into the nRF52 DK you already have. This chip does support Wi-Fi 6, though the community is still working on opening up the CSI (skeleton-tracking) hooks for it.

My recommendation: Keep the nRF52 gear for your smart home control and "last-mile" gadgets. For the skeleton tracking itself, stick with the ESP32-S3 or the Intel 5300 path—it will save you months of trying to force a Bluetooth chip to act like a high-res radar.

turns.prompt_text: So I have now 3 esp-32s and my Google Pixel phone, as well as an at-home mac mini. I am imagining using those to try to sense myposition every now and again. For now, just knowing the general room and in-room position is fine, but I would like to try the heartbeat sensing and skeleton tracking if possible, but I believe I need some form of antenna for at least one device for this
turns.response_html:
You have an incredible sandbox sitting on your desk right now. A Mac Mini paired with three ESP32s and a Pixel phone is the exact topology used in modern edge-computing and RF-sensing research. You can absolutely build a functional localization and vital-sign tracking grid with this exact stack.

The hardware and antenna requirements break down into a straightforward engineering pipeline.

1. The Antenna Question: What Do You Actually Need?

To achieve basic room presence or multi-room tracking, standard onboard PCB antennas (the little zig-zag metal traces on the ESP32 boards) will work perfectly fine.

However, once you transition to heartbeat sensing and 17-point skeleton tracking, your hardware requirements change. You are trying to capture sub-millimeter physical shifts, which means you need to maximize your Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR).

Do you need external antennas?

Yes, for the high-granularity tasks. * The Problem with PCB Antennas: Onboard traces are omnidirectional and pick up a massive amount of reflections from the floor, ceiling, and structural metal in the walls. This creates destructive multipath interference that can wash out the tiny phase shifts caused by a beating heart.

  • The Solution: You should equip at least your primary Receiver (Rx) node with an external antenna.

What type of antenna?

Instead of a standard rubber ducky antenna, look for a Directional Panel Antenna or a Patch Antenna tuned for 2.4 GHz/5 GHz.

Why Directional? By pointing a directional antenna directly across your living space toward your transmitter node, you create a high-intensity Fresnel Zone right where you sit or sleep. This acts like a spotlight, heavily amplifying the radio distortions caused by your body while ignoring the ambient noise behind the antenna.

Note: Make sure your ESP32 boards have a tiny U.FL connector on them to plug in an external antenna. If they only have the printed PCB trace, you can easily find "ESP32-S3-WROOM-1U" modules (the 'U' denotes the U.FL connector) online for a few dollars.

2. Architecting Your Local Array

With three ESP32s and a Mac Mini, your system architecture fits cleanly into an optimized edge computing pipeline:

[ ESP32 Node 1: Tx ]           [ Pixel Phone ] 
     (Pings)                  (Moving Target)
        \                           /
         v                         v
[ ESP32 Node 2: Rx ] -------> [ Mac Mini ] -------> [ Local Dashboard ]
[ ESP32 Node 3: Rx ]   UDP   (Rust Processing,      (p5.js Visualizer /
 (External Antennas)  Stream  Hampel Filtering,     17-Point Skeleton)
                             Model Inference)

Node 1: The Illuminator (Tx)

Place this ESP32 in a fixed location on one side of the room. Its sole job is to broadcast continuous, high-frequency Wi-Fi packets (usually using ESP-NOW protocols or standard dummy pings) at roughly 40 Hz to 100 Hz.

Nodes 2 & 3: The Observers (Rx)

Place these on the opposite side of the space, spaced a few feet apart to get spatial diversity (different angles). These nodes capture the raw binary data arrays representing the Channel State Information (CSI) for every single packet sent by Node 1. They instantly pipe this raw data over your local network via a fast, unencrypted UDP stream directly to your Mac Mini.

The Mac Mini: The Processing Engine

This is where the mathematical heavy lifting happens. Raw radio waves are incredibly chaotic, so your Mac Mini acts as the central signal processing backend:

  1. Hampel Filtering & Outlier Removal: Cleans up the sudden spikes caused by transient network traffic or appliance noise.
  2. Fast Fourier Transforms (FFT): Isorates the low-frequency bands. If it spots a constant sub-carrier oscillation between 0.1 Hz and 0.5 Hz, that’s your breathing. A fainter vibration between 0.8 Hz and 2.0 Hz isolates your pulse.
  3. Model Inference: Feeds the cleaned data streams into a local python/docker pipeline.

3. Launching Your System

To avoid writing complex driver hacks from scratch, leverage open-source frameworks to handle the core data collection:

  • The Framework: Clone the active RuView or ESP32-CSI-Tool repositories on GitHub. They provide pre-built firmware for the ESP32s that handles the high-speed data capture right out of the box, as well as local backend architectures optimized for macOS.
  • The 17-Point Skeleton Baseline: The open-source versions of these frameworks often integrate lightweight models like WiFlow or quantized DensePose checkpoints. When you deploy the stack locally, your Mac Mini will ingest the raw UDP arrays from your ESP32 mesh and translate those signal patterns directly into standard spatial coordinates.
  • The Phone Factor: Your Google Pixel can act as an awesome calibration tool. By running a simple script on your phone that logs its exact GPS/accelerometer position via local WebSockets to your Mac while you walk around, you can map those known spatial coordinates against your incoming Wi-Fi CSI data to fine-tune the system's spatial accuracy for your exact room layout.

turns.response_html:
No major financial investments or premium subscriptions are required to make this work. Because the open-source community has heavily optimized the processing pipelines (such as RuView and WiFi-DensePose), you can build a highly accurate grid using incredibly affordable hardware accessories.

The exact shopping list required to transition your 3 ESP32s and Mac Mini into a functional skeleton and heartbeat tracker involves a few specific components.

1. The Critical Hardware Accessory: External Antennas

To extract the micro-vibrations of a heartbeat (0.1mm chest movements) out of chaotic radio waves, standard PCB antennas (the built-in trace lines) will not cut it. You must look closely at your 3 ESP32 boards to check how they handle external antennas.

Look for the U.FL Connector

Check your ESP32 boards for a tiny, circular gold or silver receptacle about 2mm wide. This is a U.FL (IPEX) connector.

  • If your boards have the connector: You are ready to plug in external antennas.
  • If they only have the zig-zag printed line: You will need to order new variant boards specifically designated with a "U" in the model name (e.g., ESP32-S3-WROOM-1U), which cost about $4 to $6 each.

What Antennas to Buy (The "Radar" Setup)

You need to buy two cheap items to upgrade your nodes:

  1. U.FL to SMA Pigtail Cables (Pack of 3 — Approx. $6): These tiny mini-cables snap directly onto the ESP32 board and convert the fragile micro-port into a heavy-duty, threaded brass screw terminal (SMA) that can host standard antennas.
  2. 2.4GHz / 5.8GHz Directional Patch or Panel Antennas (Qty: 2 — Approx. $10–$15 each): Instead of standard "rubber ducky" stick antennas, buy flat, square directional patch antennas (often sold for drone video receivers or specialized Wi-Fi extensions).

Why Directional? Standard antennas listen to the entire room, including your spinning refrigerator compressor and metal window frames. A directional patch antenna behaves like a physical spotlight. By pointing it right at your bed or desk chair, it vastly multiplies the Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR) for that exact physical space, making heartbeats and skeletal joints visible to the AI.

2. Power and Interface Accessories

To distribute 3 nodes across a room, you need an elegant way to power and anchor them:

  • USB-C Data Cables (Qty: 3): Ensure at least one is a high-quality data-sync cable for flashing the initial firmware from your Mac Mini. The other two can just be power cables.
  • Basic USB Power Bricks: You do not need expensive adapters; any old 5V phone charger block or multi-port USB hub will easily supply the low milliamps these boards draw.
  • A Small Roll of Heavy-Duty Mounting Tape or Velcro: To prevent the weight of the external antenna cables from pulling your lightweight ESP32 boards off the wall, you must tape or securely mount the nodes in fixed, stable positions. If a node wobbles or shifts even a fraction of a millimeter during operation, the AI model will misinterpret the movement as a human ghost moving in the room.

3. The Software Cost: $0 (Completely Free)

You do not need to buy proprietary subscriptions or enterprise licenses.

Your Mac Mini handles the computational heavy lifting natively. The production-ready repositories for this architecture are entirely open-source:

  • The local Rust-based aggregators handle thousands of incoming UDP frames per second with a negligible memory footprint.
  • The pre-trained DensePose neural network weights are hosted publicly on Hugging Face and can be downloaded directly to your local system.

Your Exact Checkout Total: ~ $25 to $35

If your current ESP32 boards already have the U.FL connectors, your total out-of-pocket cost to build a high-fidelity through-wall tracking environment is literally the price of a couple of pigtail adapters and two flat directional patch antennas.

turns.prompt_text: The squares are pretty expensive, I'm going to stick to the stick antennas for now
turns.response_html:
You are making a smart engineering pivot. Those high-end flat square antennas are often overpriced for hobby experimentation. Standard "stick" antennas (known technically as dipole omnidirectional antennas) are incredibly cheap, highly reliable, and easily accessible.

However, since you are hunting for human skeletons and heartbeats rather than just basic Wi-Fi connectivity, there is a specific style of indoor stick antenna you should look out for.

The Trick to Stick Antennas: "High-Gain" vs. "Low-Gain"

Standard stick antennas are omnidirectional—they broadcast and listen in a $360^{\circ}$ ring, like a flat donut. For vital-sign and skeleton sensing, you want that "donut" to be as flat and concentrated as possible to slice cleanly through the room.

  • Low-Gain (2 dBi to 3 dBi): These are the short, stubby sticks that come standard on cheap IoT devices. Their radio pattern is shaped like a round beach ball. They capture reflections from your ceiling, your floor, and your furniture equally, which floods your Mac Mini with chaotic signal noise. Avoid these for vital sensing.
  • High-Gain (7 dBi to 9 dBi): These are much longer stick antennas (often 10 to 15 inches long). Because of their internal electrical design, they mechanically squash the radio wave pattern flat. The "beach ball" becomes a thin, razor-sharp pancake.

Why this works for your project: If you mount a long 9 dBi stick antenna vertically on your wall at chest height, its radio pattern will shoot straight across the room in a flat, horizontal slice. It will completely ignore chaotic signal reflections bouncing off your ceiling and floor, maximizing your Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR) right where your body moves.

Low-Cost Directional Stick Alternatves

If you still want a focused directional beam without the massive price tag of a square panel, look for an Indoor Directional Paddle like the Alfa APA-M25 Dual-Band Directional Antenna.

While it looks like a flat paddle, it is mechanically identical to a stick antenna inside, but it features a tiny, built-in metal reflector plate on the back. It costs around $9 to $15, screws directly onto a standard RP-SMA pigtail, and completely blocks out the radio noise behind it, focusing all its listening power in a $60^{\circ}$ cone right toward your tracking area.

Finding the Right Adapters

When ordering your stick antennas or paddles on Amazon or eBay, ensure you double-check the connector naming conventions:

  • Most generic external Wi-Fi antennas use an RP-SMA Male connector (a threaded brass barrel with a hole in the center).
  • Make sure your tiny U.FL to SMA pigtail cables match this exactly by ordering U.FL to RP-SMA Female cables (the ones with the little pin sticking out of the middle).

If you stick to long, high-gain 9 dBi dipole sticks or a cheap Alfa paddle, your total hardware expansion cost drops to roughly $10 to $15 total for the entire grid.
